question: A 3-day-old newborn is brought to the physician because of abdominal distention, inconsolable crying, and 3 episodes of bilious vomiting since the previous evening. He was delivered at home at 40 weeks' gestation by a trained midwife. He has not passed meconium. Physical examination shows abdominal distention, a tight anal sphincter, and an explosive passage of air and feces on removal of the examining finger. Abnormal development of which of the following best explains this patient's condition?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Absence of meconium passage -> intestinal obstruction -> abdominal distention, bilious vomiting, inconsolable crying -> possible Hirschsprung disease -> 80% confidence. CHAIN: Tight anal sphincter -> explosive passage of air and feces on rectal examination -> possible Hirschsprung disease -> 70% confidence. CHAIN: Home delivery by a trained midwife -> lack of proper medical assessment at birth -> missed signs of Hirschsprung disease -> 80%
analysis: The patient's presentation with abdominal distention, bilious vomiting, failure to pass meconium, and tight anal sphincter is indicative of a condition known as Hirschsprung disease. This congenital disorder is characterized by the absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses of the distal colon, leading to functional obstruction.
